items.title: The 1833 Factory Act created the first state inspectorate
items.claim: What was the significance of the 1833 Factory Act?

options.text: It prohibited textile factory employment of children under 9, limited 9-13 year olds to 9 hours/day and 13-18 year olds to 12 hours, required two hours of schooling daily — and created four paid factory inspectors with powers of entry
It applied only to coal mines
It was repealed within a year

items.reveal:
Earlier factory acts (1802 Health and Morals of Apprentices Act, 1819 Cotton Mills Act) had been largely unenforced. The 1833 Act, drafted under Lord Althorp, created the first national factory inspectorate — a tiny force initially but a precedent for state enforcement of working conditions.

Lord Ashley (later 7th Earl of Shaftesbury) campaigned for the Ten Hours Movement, achieved in 1847 (Ten Hours Act). The Mines Act 1842 banned women and children underground.

The inspectors' annual reports — read by Marx in the British Museum — provided detailed evidence of factory conditions that shaped political argument for decades.
items.why: The modern regulatory state is built up Act by Act. The 1833 inspectorate is a small institutional innovation that became a template for state oversight of every industry that followed.

items.title: London had no professional police force until 1829
items.claim: Who founded the Metropolitan Police and on what principles?

options.text: Home Secretary Robert Peel, Metropolitan Police Act 1829, with the principle that police derive authority from public consent — Peel's 'nine principles'
The Duke of Wellington as PM, modelled on military regiments

items.reveal:
The Met began with around 1,000 officers based at Scotland Yard. Uniforms were deliberately civilian-looking (blue, not the military red) to distinguish them from soldiers. Officers carried truncheons, not firearms.

The Fielding brothers' Bow Street Runners (1750) had been a small detective force. Peel's innovation was preventive uniformed patrol, full-time and salaried. Within decades every English borough had a force; the County Police Acts of 1839 and 1856 extended it nationwide.

Peel's nine principles — including 'the police are the public and the public are the police' — are still cited.
items.why: Modern policing is younger than the Industrial Revolution. The concept of a professional, preventive, public force is an early 19th-century invention with specific design choices that still shape British policing.

items.title: Magna Carta was annulled within ten weeks
items.claim: King John sealed Magna Carta at Runnymede on 15 June 1215. What happened next?

options.text: It immediately became the basis of English liberty and was respected by the crown
John wrote to Pope Innocent III, who annulled it as 'shameful and demeaning' on 24 August 1215 — civil war resumed
John was forced to confirm it in Parliament the following year
It was burned by the barons after John refused to enforce it

items.reveal:
Pope Innocent III's bull of 24 August 1215 declared Magna Carta 'null and void of all validity forever', calling it extorted by force. The First Barons' War followed; the barons invited Prince Louis of France to take the throne.

John died of dysentery in October 1216. The charter was reissued by the regents of his nine-year-old son Henry III to win support — that is the version that took root. The 1297 reissue under Edward I is the one on the statute roll.
items.why: Magna Carta as 'the foundation of liberty' is a 17th-century invention (Coke). In 1215 it was a peace treaty between a desperate king and rebellious barons — and it failed within weeks.
